claim: DMD-4 is one of ten DMRT proteins encoded by the C. elegans genome.
source: DMD-4 is one of ten DMRT proteins encoded by the C. elegans genome, only two of which, DMD-4 and DMD-5, are phylogenetically conserved in vertebrates (Volff et al., 2003; Wexler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: DMD-4 and DMD-5 are phylogenetically conserved in vertebrates.
source: DMD-4 is one of ten DMRT proteins encoded by the C. elegans genome, only two of which, DMD-4 and DMD-5, are phylogenetically conserved in vertebrates (Volff et al., 2003; Wexler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: Neither the expression nor the function of DMD-4 have previously been described.
source: Neither the expression nor the function of DMD-4 have previously been described.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the novelty of the work.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in PHA and PHB phasmid sensory neuron pairs of adult hermaphrodites, but not adult males.
source: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in PHA and PHB phasmid sensory neuron pairs of adult hermaphrodites, but not adult males (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: PHA and PHB neurons display highly dimorphic synaptic connectivity.
source: Electron micrographic reconstruction of the synaptic connectivity of males and hermaphrodites revealed that these neurons display highly dimorphic synaptic connectivity (Cook et al., 2019; Jarrell et al., 2012; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data from cited studies and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG) in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in the head mesodermal cell (hmc) in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8) in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP is expressed in four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells in a sexually non-dimorphic manner.
source: In addition to this sexually dimorphic expression, we observed sexually non-dimorphic expression of DMD-4 in a subset of head sensory neurons (AFD, AWB, AWC, ASE, ASG, ASH, BAG), a single pharyngeal neuron (I5) and a number of MS blastomere derived cells - the head mesodermal cell (hmc), a single pharyngeal muscle (pm8), a pharyngeal gland cell pair (g2L/R) and four of the six pharyngeal intestinal valve cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DMD-4::GFP fluorescence is first detectable in mid-embryonic development.
source: DMD-4::GFP fluorescence is first detectable in mid-embryonic development, with a pattern that is restricted to all the pharyngeal and the hmc cells described above.
evidence: This is based on developmental time-course microscopy observations.

claim: Onset of DMD-4::GFP expression in the non-pharyngeal nervous system is first observed at around hatching.
source: Onset of expression in the non-pharyngeal nervous system is first observed at around hatching in the same set of head and tail sensory neurons as observed in the adult stage, including the phasmid neurons PHA and PHB.
evidence: This is based on developmental time-course microscopy observations.

claim: DMD-4::GFP protein starts to disappear from PHA and PHB in the male at the L4 to adult molt, but not in the hermaphrodite.
source: During larval development, dmd-4::gfp expression is the same in both sexes until the L4 to adult molt when DMD-4::GFP protein starts to disappear from PHA and PHB in the male, but not the hermaphrodite (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time-course microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sexually dimorphic dmd-4::gfp expression in the adult PHA and PHB neurons is the result of male-specific downregulation of dmd-4::gfp from these neurons.
source: We conclude that sexually dimorphic dmd-4::gfp expression in the adult PHA and PHB neurons is the result of male-specific downregulation of dmd-4::gfp from these neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental time-course data showing loss of expression in males but not hermaphrodites.

claim: The dmd-4(ot933) putative null allele results in highly penetrant embryonic lethality.
source: This putative null allele (ot933) results in highly penetrant embryonic lethality (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryonic lethality shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The dmd-4(tm1951) deletion allele results in lethality.
source: A deletion allele generated by the C. elegans knockout consortium (tm1951), that eliminates parts of the DM domain, also results in lethality.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the phenotype of this allele.

claim: Null mutant dmd-4 animals that escape embryonic lethality are scrawny and display a stuffed anterior intestine.
source: Null mutant animals that escape embryonic lethality are scrawny and display a stuffed anterior intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The hmc fails to express arg-1::gfp in dmd-4 mutants.
source: The stuffed anterior intestine may relate to developmental defects of the hmc, which fail to express a cell fate marker (arg-1::gfp) in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dmd-4(ot896) allele results in no embryonic lethality.
source: Another deletion allele that we generated using CRISPR/Cas9 leaves the DNA binding domain unaffected, but deletes other domains of the protein (DMA domain and EH1 domain)(Figure 2A), but this allele (ot896) results in no embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the phenotype of this allele.

claim: The third intron of the dmd-4 locus contains the cis-regulatory information for all nervous system expression.
source: Through the fusion of individual segments of the dmd-4 locus to gfp, we identified the third intron of the dmd-4 locus as containing the cis-regulatory information for all nervous system expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by transgenic reporter assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) animals, dmd-4::gfp expression is lost in all head and tail neurons at all developmental stages.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering, we deleted this enhancer in the context of the dmd-4::gfp allele (dmd-4(ot957ot935)), and indeed found that in these animals dmd-4::gfp expression was lost in all head and tail neurons at all developmental stages, but unaffected in the pharynx and hmc (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants show none of the lethality or intestinal stuffing phenotypes associated with removal of the gene from all tissues.
source: Most importantly, dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants showed none of the lethality or intestinal stuffing phenotypes associated with removal of the gene from all tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), allowing us to characterize the function of dmd-4 in the nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: All head sensory neurons and phasmid neurons are generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites.
source: We found no evidence of defects in general neuronal specification or morphology; all head sensory neurons as well as the phasmid neurons were generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites and had a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites have a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies.
source: We found no evidence of defects in general neuronal specification or morphology; all head sensory neurons as well as the phasmid neurons were generated in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites and had a normal appearance of axon and dendrite morphologies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no loss or misexpression of neurotransmitter identity, neuropeptides, and receptors in the amphid and phasmid neurons of dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals.
source: Furthermore, we examined transgenic reporters for neurotransmitter identity, neuropeptides, and receptors, and found no loss or misexpression of these genes in the amphid and phasmid neurons of dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Behaviors associated with the function of head amphid sensory neurons appear unaffected in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals.
source: Lastly, behaviors associated with the function of head amphid sensory neurons also appear unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PHA and PHB neurons display dimorphic synaptic connections to neurons that are shared between the two sexes.
source: Not only do both the PHA and PHB neurons generate synaptic connections to male-specific neurons, but they also display dimorphic synaptic connections to neurons that are shared between the two sexes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Juvenile stages of C. elegans exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity in phasmid neurons.
source: We have previously used in vivo synapse labeling techniques, GRASP (GFP-Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners)(Feinberg et al., 2008) and iBLINC (Desbois et al., 2015), to show that juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity and that during sexual maturation, some synapses are then pruned, while others are maintained (Figure 3A; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP and iBLINC data from a previous study and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During sexual maturation, some phasmid neuron synapses are pruned, while others are maintained.
source: We have previously used in vivo synapse labeling techniques, GRASP (GFP-Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners)(Feinberg et al., 2008) and iBLINC (Desbois et al., 2015), to show that juvenile stages exhibit non-dimorphic 'sex-hybrid' connectivity and that during sexual maturation, some synapses are then pruned, while others are maintained (Figure 3A; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP and iBLINC data from a previous study and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Synaptic maintenance in phasmid neurons is not dependent on sex-specific patterns of neuronal activity.
source: Unlike many pruning/maintenance events during nervous system development in other animal species (Katz and Callaway, 1992; Katz and Shatz, 1996; Morgan et al., 2011; Vonhoff and Keshishian, 2017), this synaptic maintenance is not dependent on sex-specific patterns of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by genetic silencing experiments and unc-13 mutant analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons does not affect sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance.
source: We arrived at this conclusion by genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons or reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals, neither of which affects sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals does not affect sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance.
source: We arrived at this conclusion by genetic silencing of the phasmid neurons or reducing synaptic signaling in unc-13 mutant animals, neither of which affects sexually dimorphic synapse pruning/maintenance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hermaphrodite-specific connections between PHB>AVA and PHA>AVG are unaffected in dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutants.
source: While hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connections (between PHA>AVG and PHB>AVA) are unaffected in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) failed to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) fail to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants.
source: While hermaphrodite-specific synaptic connections (between PHA>AVG and PHB>AVA) are unaffected in dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), male-specific synapses (PHB>AVG) failed to be pruned in hermaphrodite dmd-4 mutants (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Wild-type males display more PHA synaptic outputs than wild-type hermaphrodites.
source: Transgenic animals show the predicted sexual dimorphism based on electron micrographic reconstruction of PHA synaptic connectivity, with wild-type males displaying more synaptic outputs than wild-type hermaphrodites (Figure 1C, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Cook et al., 2019; Jarrell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by RAB-3 puncta quantification and electron microscopy data.

claim: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals, the sexual dimorphism of PHA synaptic output is lost.
source: In dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant animals this sexual dimorphism is also lost, corroborating the notion that synapses fail to be pruned (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RAB-3 puncta quantification shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expressing dmd-4 cDNA under the control of a PHB-specific promoter rescues the PHB>AVG synaptic pruning defect.
source: We rescued the PHB>AVG synaptic pruning defect by expressing dmd-4 cDNA under the control of a PHB-specific promoter, confirming the cell-autonomous role of dmd-4 in the presynaptic neuron to control sex-specific synaptic pruning (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: dmd-4 functions in the phasmid neurons to promote pruning of phasmid synaptic connections in hermaphrodite animals during sexual maturation.
source: Taken together our results indicate that dmd-4 functions in the phasmid neurons to promote pruning of phasmid synaptic connections in hermaphrodite animals during sexual maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotype and rescue data.

claim: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior.
source: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior (Hilliard et al., 2002; Zou et al., 2017), a functional output which is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chemosensory avoidance behavior mediated by phasmid neurons is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males.
source: In larval animals, the phasmid neurons function to mediate chemosensory avoidance behavior (Hilliard et al., 2002; Zou et al., 2017), a functional output which is maintained in adult hermaphrodites, but lost in adult males (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: dmd-4 mutants exhibit no defects in SDS avoidance in juvenile stages, before sexual maturation.
source: dmd-4 mutants exhibit no defects in SDS avoidance in juvenile stages, before sexual maturation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: As adults, dmd-4 mutant hermaphrodites display a partial masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
source: However, as adults, these animals display a partial masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior, such that mutant hermaphrodites were less responsive to the noxious stimulus, although still intermediate relative to control adult males (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In ceh-14 null mutants, dmd-4::gfp expression is selectively lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes during larval stages and in the adult stage in hermaphrodites.
source: We find that in ceh-14 null mutants, dmd-4::gfp expression is selectively lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes during larval stages and in the adult stage in hermaphrodites (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
source: This is also consistent with the observation that dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior (Figure 4A), a phenotype observed in ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 4A and citation to prior work.

claim: ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior.
source: This is also consistent with the observation that dmd-4(ot957ot935) mutant hermaphrodites display masculinization of SDS avoidance behavior (Figure 4A), a phenotype observed in ceh-14 mutant hermaphrodites (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Constitutive, panneuronal expression of LIN-41 maintains DMD-4 in the adult male phasmids.
source: We generated transgenic animals that constitutively express LIN-41 in the nervous system and asked whether ectopically maintaining LIN-41 throughout all larval stages to adulthood is sufficient to maintain DMD-4 expression in the adult male phasmids. Indeed, we found that DMD-4 was ectopically maintained in these transgenic male animals (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
source: We generated transgenic animals that constitutively express LIN-41 in the nervous system and asked whether ectopically maintaining LIN-41 throughout all larval stages to adulthood is sufficient to maintain DMD-4 expression in the adult male phasmids. Indeed, we found that DMD-4 was ectopically maintained in these transgenic male animals (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the heterochronic pathway functions to regulate the timing of DMD-4 degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the LIN-41 overexpression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genetic removal of tra-1 in tra-1(e1099) XX pseudomales leads to a downregulation of DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons at the adult stage.
source: We found that genetic removal of tra-1, in tra-1(e1099) XX pseudomales, leads to a downregulation of DMD-4 expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons at the adult stage (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Force-expression of an engineered, activated version of the TRA-1 protein in the phasmid neurons of both sexes results in ectopic DMD-4 expression in male phasmid neurons.
source: Conversely, force-expression of an engineered, activated version of the TRA-1 protein which escapes protein degradation (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006) in the phasmid neurons of both sexes results in ectopic DMD-4 expression in male phasmid neurons (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation.
source: We conclude that the transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation, while its absence in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tra-1 mutant and overexpression data.

claim: The absence of TRA-1 in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
source: We conclude that the transcriptional regulator TRA-1 normally acts to promote DMD-4::GFP expression in hermaphrodite phasmid neurons upon sexual maturation, while its absence in adult male phasmids results in DMD-4 loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tra-1 mutant and overexpression data.

claim: The transcriptional reporter containing the nervous system enhancer for dmd-4 expression is expressed in the phasmid neurons of both adult hermaphrodite and adult male animals.
source: However, in the context of our analysis of the cis-regulatory control regions of dmd-4 expression, we noted that the transcriptional reporter containing the nervous system enhancer for dmd-4 expression (Figure 2B), was expressed in the phasmid neurons of both adult hermaphrodite and adult male animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The regulatory information generating DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not encoded on the transcriptional level.
source: This suggested that the regulatory information generating DMD-4 sexual dimorphism is not encoded on the transcriptional level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the transcriptional reporter is not dimorphic.

claim: Expressing gfp tagged dmd-4 cDNA with a heterologous 3' UTR under control of a non-dimorphic PHA-specific and PHB-specific promoter shows dimorphic GFP fluorescence in the phasmid neurons.
source: To define the potential mechanism of posttranscriptional regulation, we expressed gfp tagged dmd-4 cDNA with a heterologous 3' UTR under control of a non-dimorphic PHA-specific and PHB-specific promoter. In transgenic animals, these constructs show dimorphic GFP fluorescence in the phasmid neurons, identical to the endogenous DMD-4::GFP expression pattern (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation.
source: Since the dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation, sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the cDNA with heterologous UTR is still dimorphic.

claim: Sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
source: Since the dmd-4 cDNA alone confers male-specific downregulation, sexually dimorphic DMD-4 presence may be controlled on the level of stability/degradation of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the cDNA with heterologous UTR is still dimorphic.

claim: The DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains.
source: Pairwise alignments of profile hidden Markov models using HHsearch (Soding, 2005) reveals that the DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (for coupling of ubiquitin to ER degradation), a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains (Kang et al., 2003; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by computational sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CUE domains are a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains.
source: Pairwise alignments of profile hidden Markov models using HHsearch (Soding, 2005) reveals that the DMA domain shows sequence similarity to CUE domains (for coupling of ubiquitin to ER degradation), a subtype of the ubiquitin-associated (UBA) family of domains (Kang et al., 2003; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices.
source: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices; by analogy with CUE domains, helices 1 and 3 would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
evidence: This is based on the homology model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Helices 1 and 3 of the DMA domain would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
source: The DMA domain contains three alpha-helices; by analogy with CUE domains, helices 1 and 3 would be expected to form a binding surface for direct non-covalent contact with ubiquitin.
evidence: This is an inference based on analogy with CUE domains and the homology model.

claim: The C. elegans DMD-4 DMA domain binds to monoubiquitin.
source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The human DMRT3 DMA domain binds to monoubiquitin.
source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The L31R mutation in the DMA domain abolishes binding to monoubiquitin.
source: SPR binding analysis of the C. elegans dmd-4 and human Dmrt3 DMA domains shows that both bind to monoubiquitin, and this binding is lost in the L31R mutation (see panel A).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM.
source: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM, which is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding (Hurley et al., 2006; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The affinity of the DMD-4 DMA domain for ubiquitin is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding.
source: The DMD-4 DMA domain bound monoubiquitin with an affinity of ~400 µM, which is similar to known affinities for CUE-ubiquitin binding (Hurley et al., 2006; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to literature values.

claim: The DMA domain of DMD-4 behaves as a monomer.
source: Testing whether the DMA domain of DMD-4 may display the same feature, we used size exclusion chromatography with multi-angle static light scattering (SEC-MALS). We found that the DMD-4 DMA domain behaves as a monomer (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The in vitro binding of the L31R mutated DMA domain to ubiquitin was disrupted, with the affinity reduced from 404 µM to >3 mM.
source: As expected, the in vitro binding of the mutated DMA domain to ubiquitin was disrupted, with the affinity of mutant DMD-4 DMA for ubiquitin reduced from 404 µ﻿M to >3 mM (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression is lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes and at all stages of development.
source: Much to our surprise, we observed the exact opposite result; we find that in dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression is lost in the phasmid neurons in both sexes and at all stages of development (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals, DMD-4 expression in the head sensory neurons is lost in both sexes of all stages.
source: Expression in the head sensory neurons was also lost, again in both sexes of all stages.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations of the ot990 mutant.

claim: The ot990 allele results in defective pruning on the PHB>AVG synaptic connection in hermaphrodites.
source: Consistent with the phenotype of the ot957 null allele, the ot990 allele also results in defective pruning on the PHB>AVG synaptic connection in hermaphrodites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by GRASP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The binding of the DMD-4 DMA domain to ubiquitin is required to promote the stability of DMD-4 in the nervous system.
source: This suggests that the binding of the DMD-4 DMA domain to ubiquitin is required to promote the stability of DMD-4 in the nervous system, and that degradation of DMD-4 in the male phasmids at the larval to adult transition is possibly generated by loss of the ubiquitin-based stabilization mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that disrupting ubiquitin binding leads to loss of DMD-4.

claim: Degradation of DMD-4 in the male phasmids at the larval to adult transition is possibly generated by loss of the ubiquitin-based stabilization mechanism.
source: This suggests that the binding of the DMD-4 DMA domain to ubiquitin is required to promote the stability of DMD-4 in the nervous system, and that degradation of DMD-4 in the male phasmids at the larval to adult transition is possibly generated by loss of the ubiquitin-based stabilization mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: The DMA domain mutation that disrupts ubiquitin binding does not affect expression or DMD-4::GFP stability in the alimentary system throughout embryonic and larval development.
source: Intriguingly, the DMA domain mutation that disrupts ubiquitin binding does not affect expression or DMD-4::GFP stability in the alimentary system (pharynx and hmc) throughout embryonic and larval development; however, expression is reduced at the larval to adult transition (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: DMD-4::GFP expression in the alimentary system is reduced at the larval to adult transition in the ot990 mutant.
source: Intriguingly, the DMA domain mutation that disrupts ubiquitin binding does not affect expression or DMD-4::GFP stability in the alimentary system (pharynx and hmc) throughout embryonic and larval development; however, expression is reduced at the larval to adult transition (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals do not display the embryonic lethality associated with dmd-4 null alleles.
source: Hence, these animals do not display the embryonic lethality associated with dmd-4 null alleles and in spite of the reduction of protein in the adult, they show no stuffed anterior intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: dmd-4(ot990ot935) animals show no stuffed anterior intestine.
source: Hence, these animals do not display the embryonic lethality associated with dmd-4 null alleles and in spite of the reduction of protein in the adult, they show no stuffed anterior intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The ot966, ot967 and ot968 alleles behave similarly to the Leu>Arg missense mutation that is predicted to disrupt ubiquitin binding.
source: We find that these alleles behave similarly to the Leu>Arg missense mutation that is predicted to disrupt ubiquitin binding. DMD-4::GFP is destabilized in the somatic nervous system of both sexes at all stages, but expression in alimentary tissue is unaffected during embryonic and larval development (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The stability of DMD-4 in both neurons and non-neuronal tissues is promoted by ubiquitin binding to the DMA domain.
source: Taken together, the stability of DMD-4 in both neurons and non-neuronal tissues is promoted by ubiquitin binding to the DMA domain, but the need to promote DMD-4 stability by ubiquitin binding is different in different tissues and at different times (permanently in the nervous system, but not until adulthood in the alimentary system).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes.

claim: The need to promote DMD-4 stability by ubiquitin binding is different in different tissues and at different times.
source: Taken together, the stability of DMD-4 in both neurons and non-neuronal tissues is promoted by ubiquitin binding to the DMA domain, but the need to promote DMD-4 stability by ubiquitin binding is different in different tissues and at different times (permanently in the nervous system, but not until adulthood in the alimentary system).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutant phenotypes.

claim: The purified DMA domain of human DMRT3 binds ubiquitin in vitro with an affinity similar to that of the DMD-4 DMA domain.
source: We find that the purified DMA domain of human DMRT3 also binds ubiquitin in vitro through SPR analysis, with an affinity similar to that of the DMD-4 DMA domain (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The DMRT3 DMA domain can homodimerize.
source: However, unlike DMD-4, but like other CUE domains, the DMRT3 domain can homodimerize (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by SEC-MALS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Human DMRT3::GFP is not degraded in the amphid head neurons.
source: We found that like DMD-4, hDMRT3::GFP is not degraded in the amphid head neurons, but that in phasmid neurons hDMRT3::GFP is degraded (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In phasmid neurons, human DMRT3::GFP is degraded.
source: We found that like DMD-4, hDMRT3::GFP is not degraded in the amphid head neurons, but that in phasmid neurons hDMRT3::GFP is degraded (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Human DMRT3::GFP degradation in phasmid neurons appears to be not subjected to sexual or temporal control.
source: Unexpectedly, this degradation appears to be not subjected to sexual or temporal control, as we fail to observe hDMRT-3::GFP expression in the phasmid neurons of both sexes at all times (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from transgenic animals shown in Figure 7F.

claim: dmd-4 is conserved throughout the animal kingdom.
source: We have described here the expression and function of a DMRT gene, C. elegans dmd-4, that in contrast to doublesex is conserved throughout the animal kingdom and find that this gene plays a critical role in sculpting sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and prior literature.

claim: dmd-4 plays a critical role in sculpting sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity patterns.
source: We have described here the expression and function of a DMRT gene, C. elegans dmd-4, that in contrast to doublesex is conserved throughout the animal kingdom and find that this gene plays a critical role in sculpting sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is supported by the synaptic connectivity data from mutant analysis.

claim: DMD-4 protein is expressed and functions sex-specifically in the phasmid sensory neurons.
source: DMD-4 protein is expressed and functions sex-specifically in the phasmid sensory neurons where it is required to promote hermaphrodite-specific synapse pruning.
evidence: This is supported by expression and mutant analysis data.

claim: DMD-4 is required to promote hermaphrodite-specific synapse pruning.
source: DMD-4 protein is expressed and functions sex-specifically in the phasmid sensory neurons where it is required to promote hermaphrodite-specific synapse pruning.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic connectivity data from mutant analysis.

claim: Loss of DMD-4 results in aberrant maintenance of a normally sexually dimorphic synaptic connection.
source: First, loss of DMD-4 results in aberrant maintenance of a normally sexually dimorphic synaptic connection, whereas loss of DMD-5 and DMD-11 resulted in ectopic pruning of a synaptic connection.
evidence: This is supported by synaptic connectivity data from mutant analysis.

claim: Loss of DMD-5 and DMD-11 resulted in ectopic pruning of a synaptic connection.
source: First, loss of DMD-4 results in aberrant maintenance of a normally sexually dimorphic synaptic connection, whereas loss of DMD-5 and DMD-11 resulted in ectopic pruning of a synaptic connection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DMD-5 and DMD-11 function in a post-synaptic neuron (the AVG interneuron) to modulate synaptic pruning.
source: Second, DMD-5 and DMD-11 function in a post-synaptic neuron (the AVG interneuron, a sex-specific target of the phasmid neurons) to modulate synaptic pruning, whereas we find that DMD-4 functions pre-synaptically.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DMD-4 functions pre-synaptically.
source: Second, DMD-5 and DMD-11 function in a post-synaptic neuron (the AVG interneuron, a sex-specific target of the phasmid neurons) to modulate synaptic pruning, whereas we find that DMD-4 functions pre-synaptically.
evidence: This is supported by cell-specific rescue experiments.

claim: DMD-4 is present specifically in hermaphrodites.
source: Finally, DMD-4 is present specifically in hermaphrodites, which stands in contrast not only to the male-specificity of DMD-5 and DMD-11 and all other dimorphically expressed DMRT proteins in C. elegans (mab-3, mab-23, dmd-3)(Lints and Emmons, 2002; Mason et al., 2008; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by expression data.

claim: DMD-5 and DMD-11 are expressed specifically in males.
source: Finally, DMD-4 is present specifically in hermaphrodites, which stands in contrast not only to the male-specificity of DMD-5 and DMD-11 and all other dimorphically expressed DMRT proteins in C. elegans (mab-3, mab-23, dmd-3)(Lints and Emmons, 2002; Mason et al., 2008; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All other dimorphically expressed DMRT proteins in C. elegans (mab-3, mab-23, dmd-3) are expressed specifically in males.
source: Finally, DMD-4 is present specifically in hermaphrodites, which stands in contrast not only to the male-specificity of DMD-5 and DMD-11 and all other dimorphically expressed DMRT proteins in C. elegans (mab-3, mab-23, dmd-3)(Lints and Emmons, 2002; Mason et al., 2008; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: dmd-4 is required for animal viability, apparently due to a non-sexually dimorphic requirement in the feeding organ of the worm.
source: In addition to the sexually dimorphic functions in the hermaphrodite phasmid neurons, we found that dmd-4 is required for animal viability, apparently due to a non-sexually dimorphic requirement in the feeding organ of the worm.
evidence: This is supported by the lethality and stuffed intestine phenotypes of null mutants.

claim: The dmd-4 orthologs DMRT93B (Arthropods) and Dmrt3 (vertebrates) have been implicated in development of feeding organs based on both expression and function.
source: The dmd-4 orthologs DMRT93B (Arthropods) and Dmrt3 (vertebrates) have also been implicated in development of feeding organs based on both expression and function, with mouse Dmrt3 knockout mutants unable to survive past weaning due to feeding defects (Ahituv et al., 2007; Inui et al., 2017; Panara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mouse Dmrt3 knockout mutants are unable to survive past weaning due to feeding defects.
source: The dmd-4 orthologs DMRT93B (Arthropods) and Dmrt3 (vertebrates) have also been implicated in development of feeding organs based on both expression and function, with mouse Dmrt3 knockout mutants unable to survive past weaning due to feeding defects (Ahituv et al., 2007; Inui et al., 2017; Panara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Sex-specific transcription factor degradation has been observed for the TRA-1 master regulator of sexual identity in C. elegans.
source: Sex-specific transcription factor degradation is not unprecedented. Not only has it been observed for the TRA-1 master regulator of sexual identity in C. elegans (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006), but a recent study in Drosophila also revealed sex-specific degradation of the Lola transcription factor (Sato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A recent study in Drosophila revealed sex-specific degradation of the Lola transcription factor.
source: Sex-specific transcription factor degradation is not unprecedented. Not only has it been observed for the TRA-1 master regulator of sexual identity in C. elegans (Schvarzstein and Spence, 2006), but a recent study in Drosophila also revealed sex-specific degradation of the Lola transcription factor (Sato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The DMA domain is an evolutionarily ancient domain.
source: We reveal here a different mechanism that involves an evolutionarily ancient domain, the DMA domain.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The presence of a DMA domain was characteristic of the three ancestral DMRT gene clusters.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the DMRT gene family suggests that the presence of a DMA domain was characteristic of the three ancestral gene clusters, and arose before the evolution of eumetazoans, but this domain has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters (Mawaribuchi et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The DMA domain arose before the evolution of eumetazoans.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the DMRT gene family suggests that the presence of a DMA domain was characteristic of the three ancestral gene clusters, and arose before the evolution of eumetazoans, but this domain has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters (Mawaribuchi et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The DMA domain has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of the DMRT gene family suggests that the presence of a DMA domain was characteristic of the three ancestral gene clusters, and arose before the evolution of eumetazoans, but this domain has not been maintained in all extant DMRT clusters (Mawaribuchi et al., 2019; Wexler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In C. elegans, dmd-4 represents the only gene that encodes a DMA domain.
source: In C. elegans, dmd-4 represents the only gene that encodes a DMA domain, which we identify here as required for protein stability and able to bind monoubiquitin, consistent with its sequence similarity to the CUE domains of the UBA family.
evidence: This is based on genome analysis.

claim: The DMA domain is required for protein stability.
source: In C. elegans, dmd-4 represents the only gene that encodes a DMA domain, which we identify here as required for protein stability and able to bind monoubiquitin, consistent with its sequence similarity to the CUE domains of the UBA family.
evidence: This is supported by mutant analysis data.

claim: The DMA domain is able to bind monoubiquitin.
source: In C. elegans, dmd-4 represents the only gene that encodes a DMA domain, which we identify here as required for protein stability and able to bind monoubiquitin, consistent with its sequence similarity to the CUE domains of the UBA family.
evidence: This is supported by SPR binding data.

claim: H. sapiens Dmrt3 appears to be subjected to posttranslational regulation in worms.
source: We find that the H. sapiens Dmrt3 DMA domain is also able to non-covalently bind monoubiquitin and that H. sapiens Dmrt3 appears to also be subjected to posttranslational regulation in worms, suggesting a conserved molecular function of the DMA domain.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic expression data in worms.

claim: The molecular function of the DMA domain is conserved.
source: We find that the H. sapiens Dmrt3 DMA domain is also able to non-covalently bind monoubiquitin and that H. sapiens Dmrt3 appears to also be subjected to posttranslational regulation in worms, suggesting a conserved molecular function of the DMA domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of behavior between C. elegans and human proteins.

claim: CUE domains have been associated with a breadth of regulatory functions as a result of their association with ubiquitin: dimerization, subcellular trafficking, covalent ubiquitylation, and protein complex formation.
source: CUE domains have been associated with a breadth of regulatory functions as a result of their association with ubiquitin: dimerization, subcellular trafficking, covalent ubiquitylation, and protein complex formation (Bagola et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2006; Davies et al., 2003; Prag et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Certain types of non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domains have been shown to stabilize proteins.
source: Intriguingly, certain types of non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domains have been shown to stabilize proteins (Flick et al., 2006; Heessen et al., 2005; Heinen et al., 2011; Heinen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domain of the yeast transcription factor Met4 interacts with ubiquitin molecules that are covalently attached elsewhere on the protein to prevent polyubiquitin chain extension and proteasomal degradation of Met4.
source: For example, the non-covalent ubiquitin-binding domain of a yeast transcription factor, Met4, interacts with ubiquitin molecules that are covalently attached elsewhere on the protein to prevent polyubiquitin chain extension and proteasomal degradation of Met4 (Flick et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Disruption of the non-covalent ubiquitin binding domain of Met4 results in degradation of Met4.
source: Consequently, disruption of this non-covalent ubiquitin binding domain of Met4 results in degradation of Met4.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Ubiquitin binding to DMD-4 may prevent protein degradation.
source: Based on the Met4 precedent, we hypothesize that ubiquitin binding to DMD-4 may also prevent protein degradation.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to Met4.

claim: The apparently ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of DMD-4 is susceptible to three parameters: sexual identity, cell-type and time.
source: The apparently ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of DMD-4 is susceptible to three parameters: sexual identity, cell-type and time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression and mutant data.

claim: In wild-type animals, DMD-4 is only degraded in the phasmid neurons, not in other neuronal or non-neuronal cell types.
source: In wild-type animals, DMD-4 is only degraded in the phasmid neurons, not in other neuronal or non-neuronal cell types.
evidence: This is supported by expression data.

claim: DMD-4 degradation in phasmid neurons only occurs in males.
source: In addition, this degradation only occurs in males and it only occurs at a specific time of development.
evidence: This is supported by expression data.

claim: DMD-4 degradation in phasmid neurons only occurs at a specific time of development.
source: In addition, this degradation only occurs in males and it only occurs at a specific time of development.
evidence: This is supported by expression data.

claim: The DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction may be subject to dynamic control in the phasmid neurons of wildtype animals.
source: Based on the degradation of DMD-4 in phasmid neurons in both sexes at all times upon mutation of the presumptive ubiquitin binding site , we hypothesize that the DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction may be subject to dynamic control in the phasmid neurons of wildtype animals.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mutant phenotype.

claim: The stabilizing effect of ubiquitin binding may be disrupted sex-specifically in males, thereby permitting degradation of the protein.
source: For example, this stabilizing effect may be disrupted sex-specifically in males, thereby permitting degradation of the protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: An adult-specific process, controlled by the heterochronic pathway, allows the disruption of the DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction.
source: Since the forced expression of LIN-41 (and hence the forced retention of a juvenile state) suppresses DMD-4 degradation, it appears that an adult-specific process, controlled by the heterochronic pathway (e.g. a protein phosphorylation event) allows the disruption of the DMD-4/ubiquitin interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the LIN-41 overexpression data.

claim: Destabilization of DMD-4 may be the 'default state', but may be antagonized by LIN-41 in juveniles in both sexes and then by TRA-1 in adult hermaphrodites.
source: This destabilization may be the 'default state', but may be antagonized by LIN-41 in juveniles in both sexes and then by TRA-1 in adult hermaphrodites (schematized in Figure 8).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and schematized in Figure 8.

claim: Either forced expression of LIN-41 or TRA-1 prevents destabilization in male adult phasmid neuron.
source: Consistent with this notion, either forced expression of LIN-41 or TRA-1 prevents destabilization in male adult phasmid neuron.
evidence: This is supported by transgenic overexpression data.

claim: In the head sensory neurons, there appears to be no dynamic control of DMD-4 stability.
source: Strikingly, in the head sensory neurons, there appears to be no dynamic control of stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression and mutant data.

claim: In the head sensory neurons, DMD-4 may always require ubiquitin binding for its stabilization.
source: In that cellular context, DMD-4 may always require ubiquitin binding for its stabilization.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: In the pharynx and hmc, ubiquitin binding is only required in the adult stage to stabilize DMD-4 in both sexes.
source: However, in the pharynx and hmc, the situation is again different. While ubiquitin binding is also required to stabilize the protein, this binding is only required in the adult stage to stabilize DMD-4 in both sexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the ubiquitin binding mutation only destabilizes DMD-4 in adult, but not in juvenile stages.

claim: The spatial specificity of DMRT expression is controlled by terminal selector-type transcription factors that generally control neuronal identity.
source: As demonstrated before for mab-3, dmd-3 and here for dmd-4, the spatial specificity of expression (i.e. the cell types which display dimorphic DMRT expression) is controlled by terminal selector-type transcription factors that generally control neuronal identity (Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and citation to prior work.

claim: The sexual specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 is controlled by direct transcriptional repression by the TRA-1 protein, which prevents transcription of these genes in hermaphrodites.
source: The sexual specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 is controlled by direct transcriptional repression by the TRA-1 protein, which prevents transcription of these genes in hermaphrodites (Mason et al., 2008; Pereira et al., 2019; Yi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Temporal specificity of mab-3 and dmd-3 is controlled by the posttranscriptional repression of mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA via LIN-41.
source: Temporal specificity is controlled by the posttranscriptional repression of mab-3 and dmd-3 mRNA via a member of the heterochronic pathway (specifically, the mRNA binding protein LIN-41), therefore resulting in male- and adult-specific expression of MAB-3 and DMD-3 protein (Figure 8; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and schematized in Figure 8.

claim: dmd-4 is transcribed and the protein accumulates in both sexes in juvenile states.
source: In striking contrast, dmd-4 is transcribed and the protein accumulates in both sexes in juvenile states, but its sexual specificity is regulated by protein stabilization and it appears to be this protein stabilization phenomenon that is controlled by presently unknown means via the LIN-41 and TRA-1 protein (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by expression data and schematized in Figure 8.

claim: The sexual specificity of dmd-4 is regulated by protein stabilization.
source: In striking contrast, dmd-4 is transcribed and the protein accumulates in both sexes in juvenile states, but its sexual specificity is regulated by protein stabilization and it appears to be this protein stabilization phenomenon that is controlled by presently unknown means via the LIN-41 and TRA-1 protein (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by expression and mutant data and schematized in Figure 8.

claim: The protein stabilization phenomenon of dmd-4 is controlled by presently unknown means via the LIN-41 and TRA-1 protein.
source: In striking contrast, dmd-4 is transcribed and the protein accumulates in both sexes in juvenile states, but its sexual specificity is regulated by protein stabilization and it appears to be this protein stabilization phenomenon that is controlled by presently unknown means via the LIN-41 and TRA-1 protein (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and schematized in Figure 8.
